newsitem.title: KENYA: Rosy view on Africa at odds with spread of conflict.
newsitem.headline: Rosy view on Africa at odds with spread of conflict.

text.p: With applause for Laurent Kabila's takeover in Zaire still echoing, optimists in and out of Africa see a brightening future of steady economic advance and pragmatic politics for the continent.
Pessimists, however, are challenging these upbeat perceptions.
The optimists admire the coalition of leaders which toppled President Mobutu Sese Seko in May after 32 mostly kleptocratic years in charge of Africa's third largest country.
The rosy view, that time is up for incompetent dictatorship and anti-people economic policies, was strikingly painted by two World Bank vice-presidents.
"Africa is on the move. From Mali to Uganda to South Africa, hope and real success are transforming the continent," according to Callisto Madavo and Jean-Louis Sarbib.
"No-nonsense, accountable pragmatism is now the rule," they wrote in an article for the International Herald Tribune.
In its section on the outlook for Africa, the final communique of last weekend's summit of the Group of Seven most industrialised countries gave some support to the enthusiasts.
The discordant voices ,as a starting point, exclude the cluster of countries in the southern cone, saying wealthy and democratic South Africa is helping to promote stability and growth.
North Africa is also removed from the equation because its real focus is on the Arab world and Europe.
That leaves a band of 30-odd states stretching from Senegal on the Atlantic to Kenya on the Indian Ocean. Within this group, the grounds for sweeping optimism suddenly look very shaky.
"In industrial terms, very few countries are even at the level of South Korea in 1960," said Gerard Prunier, a French academic expert on eastern Africa.

He said World Bank figures showing a growth in per capita income were deceptive. The growth is barely ahead of the population rise, is skewed by South Africa's inclusion and depends largely on oil exports from Nigeria and Angola, Prunier said.
More important, the number of countries whose internal politics are in good shape is still tiny. The list invariably and plausibly starts with Ghana but quickly peters out.
The populous countries which should be dragging Africa to peace and prosperity, such as Nigeria, Sudan, Ethiopia and ex-Zaire, are incapable of doing so for disparate reasons.
Conflict has spread like a rash since Kabila was helped by a coalition of countries, led by Rwanda and Uganda, to overthrow Mobutu.
In Congo, Central African Republic and Sierra Leone, armed factional anarchy has broken out.
In Angola, a civil war that was supposed to have ended could be starting again.

Most ominously, the long-running rebellion by southerners in Sudan is gaining strength with support from Ethiopia, Eritrea, Uganda and, critically, the United States, western and African diplomats say.
Few tears were shed for Mobutu but there are awkward questions about the efficiency of his removal and the belief in Africa that the United States was fully in favour.
"There is concern that if two or three countries feel unhappy about a regime they can just remove it. Is this the start of a reconfiguration of states?" asked a senior African diplomat.

With the United Nations groping to find it role, the fabled but increasingly fictitious "international community" has shown no evidence of having the will to prevent new African conflicts or bury old ones.
The immediate danger zone is the group of former French colonies around Zaire, all of which look vulnerable because of ossified politics, corruption and ethnic fears.
"The fundamental phenomenon today is the decomposition of the French empire in Africa," Prunier said.
"State structures in francophone central Africa are collapsing," he said in an interview.
With the end of the Cold War in the late 1980s, France lost its job as the Western gendarme for nearly half of Africa.

Paris failed to adapt and lost ground first in Rwanda, then Zaire and now Congo where French troops were sent this month to evacuate foreigners. A few years ago they would have used force to defend the elected but feeble government of Pascal Lissouba.
The shake-out in central Africa looks inevitable.
Money-driven ethnic or clan militias already control Liberia and Somalia. Now Congo, Central African Republic and Sierra Leone seem to be falling victim to the scourge.
"We all applauded and legitimised a foreign-backed armed offensive in Zaire but we indicated to others that they can do the same," an experienced African aid worker said.
